'''Theory of Japan's Indigenous People''' (日本原住民論)

# A series of theories collectively referred to as "Yagiri's historical perspective," with a focus on the "Japanese indigenous people" as defined by historical novelist {{ill|Tomeo Yagiri|ja|八切止夫|qid=Q11390586}}.
# The historical perspective of Japan's New Left, which borrows and modifies Yagiri's perspective. Both are discussed in this article.

----

== Yagiri's Historical Perspective ==
Yagiri Tomio proposed various theories that overturned conventional historical wisdom. Among them was the "Theory of Japan's Indigenous People," which posited that the {{ill|Yamato Kingship|eo|Jamato (regno)|es|Reinado de Yamato|fa|پادشاهی یاماتو|fi|Yamato (valtio)|fr|Royauté de Yamato|ja|ヤマト王権|ko|야마토 정권|ru|Ямато (государство)|sr|Јамато (држава)|uk|Ямато (держава)|vi|Vương quyền Yamato|zh|大和王权|qid=Q2658252}} was an external regime and that the descendants of indigenous peoples became the {{ill|Burakumin|ar|بوراكومين|ca|Buraku|ckb|بوراکومین|cs|Burakumin|de|Buraku|eo|Burakumin|es|Burakumin|eu|Burakumin|fa|بوراکومین|fi|Burakulaiset|fr|Burakumin|hr|Burakumin|hu|Burakumin|id|Burakumin|it|Burakumin|ja|部落問題|ko|부라쿠민|lt|Burakumin|ml|ബുരാകുമിൻ|mr|बुराकुमीन|ms|Burakumin|nl|Burakumin|pl|Burakumin|pt|Burakumin|ro|Burakumin|ru|Буракумин|sl|Burakumini|sv|Burakumin|ta|புராகுமின்|tr|Burakumin|uk|Буракуміни|vi|Burakumin|zh|部落民|zh_min_nan|Burakumin|qid=Q548787}} and {{ill|Sanka (ethnic group)|ja|サンカ|ko|산카|th|ซังกะ|tr|Sankalar|zh|山窩|qid=Q4833074|lt=Sanka}} populations.<ref>The idea that the Yamato government was an external regime and that the origins of Burakumin trace back to ancient ethnic groups such as the Emishi predates Yagiri, who combined these theories.</ref>

However, Yagiri's perspective assumed that these "indigenous peoples" were historically connected to the Imperial lineage, with the {{ill|Imperial House of Japan|ar|البيت الإمبراطوري في اليابان|as|জাপানৰ ৰাজপৰিয়াল|ast|Familia imperial xaponesa|az|Yaponiya imperator evi|be|Імператарскі дом Японіі|ca|Família Imperial del Japó|ckb|خێزانی شاھانەی ژاپۆن|cs|Japonská císařská dynastie|de|Japanisches Kaiserhaus|el|Αυτοκρατορικός Οίκος της Ιαπωνίας|eo|Japana reĝa familio|es|Familia imperial japonesa|fa|دودمان یاماتو|fr|Maison impériale du Japon|he|בית הקיסרות של יפן|hr|Japanska carska obitelj|hu|Japán császári ház|id|Wangsa Kekaisaran Jepang|it|Famiglia imperiale del Giappone|ja|皇室|ko|일본 황실|la|Domus imperatoriae Iaponiae|ms|Kerabat diraja Jepun|no|Japans keiserhus|pt|Casa Imperial do Japão|ro|Familia imperială a Japoniei|ru|Японский императорский дом|sh|Carska kuća Japana|simple|Imperial House of Japan|sq|Shtëpia Perandorake e Japonisë|th|ราชวงศ์ญี่ปุ่น|tr|Yamato Hanedanı|uk|Імператорський дім Японії|ur|جاپان کا شاہی خاندان|vi|Hoàng thất Nhật Bản|zh|日本皇室|zh_classical|日本皇室|zh_min_nan|Ji̍t-pún hông-sek|zh_yue|日本皇室|qid=Q909452|lt=Imperial House of Japan}} serving as a symbol of their unity. Thus, Yagiri himself was not a proponent of leftist ideology.<ref>In Yagiri's book *History of Japan's Indigenous People*, respectful expressions towards the Imperial family, such as "His Majesty Emperor Sujin (97 BCE, pg. 13)" and "Prince Hieda, Crown Prince of Emperor Kōnin (pg. 17)," demonstrate a clear distinction from New Left ideology.</ref><ref>However, Yagiri's theories, including the idea that the Emperor descended from Arabs, show inconsistencies.</ref>

== New Left Historical Perspective ==
The "Theory of Japan's Indigenous People" was later adopted by Japan's New Left, unbeknownst to Yagiri. During his time underground, Communist League Red Army faction leader {{ill|Tsuneo Umenai|ja|梅内恒夫|ko|우메나이 쓰네오|qid=Q11538394}} was inspired by Yagiri's theory and published *To All Who Aspire to Overthrow Japanese Imperialism*. This marked a shift in the justification for "overthrowing Japanese imperialism" from the wrongdoings of the {{ill|Empire of Japan|af|Japannese Keiserryk|ar|إمبراطورية اليابان|arz|امبراطورية اليابان|ast|Imperiu del Xapón|az|Yaponiya imperiyası|azb|ژاپون ایمپیراتورلوغو|bcl|Imperyo kan Hapon|be|Японская імперыя|be_x_old|Японская імпэрыя|bg|Японска империя|bjn|Kakaisaran Japang|bn|জাপান persecution of indigenous peoples at the time of Japan's founding. {{ill|Ryu Ota|arz|ريو اوتا|fr|Ryū Ōta|ja|太田竜|ko|오타 류|ru|Ота, Рю|vi|Ota Ryu|qid=Q7385483|lt=Ryū Ōta}}, who advocated the theory of revolutionary poverty, also praised Yagiri as a "true people's historian."

Thus, New Left activists established a unique historical perspective that called for the "restoration of Japan's indigenous people." Their approach involved elevating the "phantom regional regimes" destroyed by the Yamato Court to relativize the Emperor system. This historical perspective inspired {{ill|katou saburou|ja|加藤三郎|qid=Q11398971}} and other {{ill|Non-sect radical|ja|ノンセクト・ラジカル|ko|논섹트 래디컬|qid=Q11325809}} activists to commit anti-Japanese terrorist acts and piqued their interest in the {{ill|koshi koden|ja|古史古伝|ko|고사고전|qid=Q11410976}}, texts claiming to predate the {{ill|Kojiki|ace|Kojiki|ar|كوجيكي|az|Kociki|bcl|Kojiki|be|Кодзікі|bg|Коджики|ca|Kojiki|ckb|کۆجیکی|cs|Kodžiki|da|Kojiki|de|Kojiki|eo|Koĝiki|es|Kojiki|et|Kojiki|eu|Kojiki|fa|کوجیکی|fi|Kojiki|fr|Kojiki|gl|Kojiki|he|קוג'יקי|hi|कोजिकी|hr|Kojiki|hu|Kodzsiki|hy|Կոձիկի|id|Kojiki|it|Kojiki|ja|古事記|ka|კოძიკი|kk|Кодзики|kn|ಕೋಜಿಕಿ|ko|고사기|la|Kojiki|lt|Kodžiki|mk|Коџики|ml|കൊജികി|ms|Kojiki|my|ခိုဂျိခိ|nl|Kojiki|no|Kojiki|oc|Kojiki|pl|Kojiki|pt|Kojiki|ro|Kojiki|rsk|Кодїки|ru|Кодзики|sh|Kojiki|simple|Kojiki|sk|Kodžiki|sl|Kodžiki|sr|Коџики|sv|Kojiki|ta|கோஜிகி|th|โคจิกิ|tl|Kojiki|tr|Kojiki|uk|Кодзікі|vi|Cổ sự ký|zh|古事記|zh_classical|古事記|qid=Q813031|lt=Kojiki}} and {{ill|Nihon Shoki|en|Nihon Shoki|qid=Q813935|lt=Nihon Shoki}}.

Some New Left activists,<ref>Besides Ryū Ōta, former {{ill|Bund|en|Bund|qid=Q128590|lt=Bund movement activists}} like {{ill|Sūgen Takeda|ja|武田崇元|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Takeda Sōgen|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11546163}} are notable examples.</ref> influenced by pseudo-histories, contributed to the occult boom of the 1980s. The popularity of texts like the {{ill|Tsugarusotosangunshi|ja|東日流外三郡誌|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tōno outside the Three Counties|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11527216}} was no coincidence. According to researcher {{ill|harada minoru|ja|原田実|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hajime Harada (author)|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q16284037}}, movements like {{ill|Aum Shinrikyo|en|Aum Shinrikyo|qid=Q217408|lt=Aum Shinrikyō}}, which also emerged during this time, were pseudo-historical movements influenced by these ideologies, leading to attempts at {{ill|tenpuku|ja|国家転覆|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/coup d'état|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 転覆|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11637535}}.

== Historical Interpretations ==
Although the New Left historical perspective borrows heavily from Yagiri's interpretations, their unique aspect lies in using these interpretations as a political ideology to rationalize anti-Japanese thought. Consequently, historical facts that do not align with their perspective are often ignored or altered.

; Origins of the Ainu people
:Yagiri saw the {{ill|Ainu people|ja|アイヌ民族|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ainu people|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to アイヌ|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q101828}} as a people native to Hokkaido from ancient times, separate from the "Japanese indigenous people."<ref>Later, Yagiri proposed a theory that white Ainu subjugated yellow-skinned indigenous people but were collectively conquered by newcomers from the continent.</ref> The New Left, however, included the Ainu as part of the "Japanese indigenous people," using their "enslavement" as a basis for condemning "Japan's wrongdoing."
; Origins of the Imperial House
:Both perspectives consider the Imperial House to have originated from {{ill|Toraijin|en|Toraijin|qid=Q11561926|lt=Toraijin}} rather than the "Japanese indigenous people." The New Left uses this to deny the Emperor's legitimacy as a ruler.
; Origins of the Fujiwara clan and the ritsuryō system
:The New Left claims that the {{ill|Battle of Baekgang|en|Battle of Baekgang|qid=Q608727|lt=Battle of Baekgang}} led to a Tang occupation, which established the ritsuryō system and rewrote history through the compilation of the Nihon Shoki, thus asserting their dominance.
